content: To obtain a list of staff titles and their corresponding salaries at a facility, the following steps should be taken: 1. If gross salaries are unavailable, collect the net (post-deduction) salary values. Using an estimate of the proportion of income tax and other deductions applicable to the type of employee in the country, calculate the gross salary. 2. If actual salary data cannot be collected for facilities based on the staff mix, an average salary for a cadre of staff can be used. 3. Gross annual benefits should include housing and travel allowances, hazard or incentive pay, and any other payments made to staff for their service to the facility. If a staff member works only part of the year (e.g., due to retirement, resignation, or periodic work), the gross annual salary should be adjusted proportionally to the time worked. 4. Similarly, the average working hours per week over the year should account for any time when the staff member was not working at the facility. This can be calculated by using the total hours worked during the year and finding the average weekly hours. 5. The TB Personnel section should list every staff member (both direct and support) providing TB services within the facility. If relevant, the type of healthcare worker can be modified to include their clinic or specialty (e.g., phlebotomists, pharmacists, social workers, etc.). 6. For staff costing, bottom-up costing can be performed through observation or interviews, while top-down costing uses timesheets. Observations, interviews, and timesheets should be administered to at least one staff member per cadre in large facilities. In smaller facilities with only two staff members working on TB, both should be interviewed and provided with timesheets. At least one bottom-up and one top-down estimate of staff time per service should be obtained. If observation or interview is not possible, assumptions based on interviews at another facility, standard operating procedures, or process demonstrations can be used. 7. TB service utilization data should be recorded for the 20 standardized service outputs and at least 39 diagnostic and monitoring tests being costed, as well as the drug regimens and supplies used. Estimation of unit costs requires information on utilization, which includes data on services received by patients in a facility or diagnostic tests processed in a laboratory. Examples of standard utilization data include the total number of people initiating treatment for MDR-TB using the long regimen per year, the total number of inpatient bed-days for DS-TB treatment per year, or the number of Xpert® MTB/RIF tests performed per year. 8. Service utilization data should be obtained from the head of the facility, laboratory, or radiology departments, or other personnel responsible for surveillance or service utilization reports. TB treatment data can be extracted from the TB Register or annual/quarterly reports for TB. 9. The ideal approach is to collect information on the number of visits that actually occur at a facility based on the facility's reporting. If the number of patients is known but not the number of visits, the number of visits can be calculated using the average number of visits per patient multiplied by the number of patients. 10. For test volume, if annual values are unavailable, the head of the laboratory or equivalent personnel should estimate the total TB and all tests per week, then multiply this number by 52 to obtain the annual value. This estimation should be presented to the interviewee for validation. 11. Missing data should be avoided as much as possible, as allocations cannot be calculated without complete data. If unavoidable, indicate this in the notes column. 12. The average quantity of each service output required for each patient type (population, regimen, and phase) should be obtained by interviewing the TB head nurse or another knowledgeable staff member. Ideally, this data should be extracted from patient records to calculate the average. If patient records are inaccessible, the quantities should be obtained through interviews. 13. For community vaccination visits, the total number of visits per year and the number of infants vaccinated during that year are needed to calculate the average number of people vaccinated per visit and the cost per person vaccinated. Similarly, the total visits and total people screened during the year of assessment are needed to calculate the cost per person screened. 14. For TB drugs, it is essential to understand how medication is dispensed in terms of location (e.g., clinic, hospital, outreach), frequency (e.g., daily, monthly), and the personnel involved in dispensing (e.g., pharmacist, doctor, nurse). The quantities entered should ideally reflect the actual average for all patients treated. If unavailable, protocol values for an average patient in the respective regimens can be used. 15. Staff time used for TB service delivery should be captured using three methods: interviews, observations, and timesheets. The data collection tool provides a sheet for each method. Staff timesheets should be completed for a relevant period (e.g., a month) and returned. If incomplete, interviews can be conducted to estimate time spent on tasks. Observations can also be used to time relevant services. 16. Supplies data should include an exhaustive list of supplies used for TB services at the facility, with annual expenditure and percentage use for TB collected. Wastage of supplies refers to the percentage of supplies discarded (e.g., expired or thrown out). If facility-specific values cannot be obtained, an estimated value for the country can be used. 17. Equipment and furniture data should include the name, manufacturer, model, unit price, and useful life. This data can be obtained from the facility or a central source such as the Ministry of Health.
